analysis.one_liner: Requires a federal license and registration for every handgun owner nationwide.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote; it died in the House Judiciary Committee when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require every person in the United States to obtain a federal handgun license — available only to adults 21 and older who pass a background check, submit fingerprints and a photo, and complete firearms safety training — and to register each handgun they own. States that already run a licensing and registration system meeting the same standards could keep their own, with the Attorney General certifying them. States and local governments could get federal grants to build the required systems, and the whole framework would take effect two years after enactment.
analysis.who_benefits: People at risk of handgun violence — residents of communities where illegal handguns drive shootings, and the families of victims. A licensing and registration system is designed to make it harder for prohibited people and traffickers to obtain handguns and to give police a record linking guns to owners when a crime gun is recovered. Lawful owners who comply would keep their guns under a clear national rule.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it unlawful to own or possess a handgun without a federal license and registration, with license eligibility limited to people 21 and older who are citizens, nationals, or lawful permanent residents, pass a background investigation and criminal history check, submit fingerprints and a photograph, complete safety training, and are not already barred from possessing firearms.

Licenses would expire after no more than five years, and the Attorney General must build a system that can easily retrieve information identifying each handgun owner and each handgun — a registry intended to help trace crime guns and hold traffickers accountable.

States with their own licensing and registration systems that meet the same standards — including criminal penalties for unlicensed possession and permit requirements for ammunition transfers — would be certified to keep their own systems in place of the federal one.

States, local governments, and Indian tribes could receive competitive federal grants to build or operate the licensing and registration systems, with audits every two years and annual reports to Congress, and the Attorney General is authorized to spend 'such sums as may be necessary' on the program.
Violations would carry fines, imprisonment, or both, and courts could not suspend any prison sentence imposed.

analysis.who_pays: Millions of lawful handgun owners would bear new costs: license applications, fingerprints, photographs, mandatory safety training, registration of each gun, and criminal liability — with no chance of a suspended sentence — for any lapse. Firearms manufacturers, dealers, and the broader gun trade would face a customer base reduced and slowed by licensing requirements. Taxpayers would fund the federal system and the state implementation grants, which carry no dollar cap.
analysis.who_pays_short: Handgun owners, the gun trade, taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill makes unlicensed handgun possession a federal crime for which courts 'shall not suspend a sentence of imprisonment,' so otherwise law-abiding owners — including people who owned handguns legally for decades before the law's two-year effective window closed — would face mandatory jail exposure for paperwork failures.

The bill authorizes 'such sums as may be necessary' in spending with no dollar limit, and the registration system it creates is a federal database identifying every handgun owner, which gun-rights advocates warn could be repurposed for confiscation — an objection the bill text does not answer.

The strongest good-faith objection is empirical: opponents argue that licensing and registration laws mostly burden people who follow the law and do little to stop criminals, who by definition would not register; supporters respond that registration helps police trace crime guns and that licensing with training and background checks reduces diversion of handguns to illegal markets. The record here contains no evidence resolving that dispute.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-safety aim — keeping handguns away from prohibited people and giving police a way to trace crime guns — addresses a serious problem, and the grant funding gives states a path to implement rather than fight the mandate. But the costs fall heavily on people who already own handguns lawfully: mandatory training, fingerprinting, registration of every gun, and mandatory prison exposure for violations, with the heaviest compliance burden landing on less organized, lower-income owners. The national politics were so one-sided that the question was never tested; the bill never advanced far enough for a cost-benefit debate on the record.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its crime subcommittee, and no one ever scheduled it for a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman introduced the bill on January 17, 2019, joined by Reps. Espaillat, Pallone, and Sires as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary, and on March 4, 2019 was referred further to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security.
No further action was ever taken: the committee never held a hearing or markup, the bill never reached the House floor, and it died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
Support stayed thin throughout — the bill drew 6 cosponsors, all Democrats, out of 231 House Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opponents of federal handgun licensing — the firearms industry, gun-rights organizations, and handgun owners who would have faced the new licensing and registration requirements — are better off because the bill never moved. Nothing in the record indicates the Judiciary Committee ever considered it on the merits, so the outcome reflects its lack of support in Congress rather than a tested judgment on the policy itself.

for.name: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Handgun Licensing and Registration Act of 2019 and recruited three colleagues as original cosponsors.

for.name: 6 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on and no other Democrats were recruited.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Jerrold Nadler (D-NY)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — after referral to the committee and its crime subcommittee in early 2019.

against.name: Gun-rights organizations, including the NRA
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal handgun licensing and registration, a policy long at the top of the gun-rights movement's list of red lines.

sides.party_line_note: The only recorded support was Democratic — a sponsor and 6 cosponsors, all Democrats out of 231 House Democrats — and no Republican ever signed on; no vote was ever taken, so the parties' floor positions were never tested.

industries.note: Licensing and registration requirements would slow and shrink the market for handguns by adding an eligibility screen, training, and registration before every owner, and dealers would bear compliance work under a system policed by federal law enforcement. Their interest in keeping sales friction-free ran against the bill's public-safety goal.

The bill requires completed firearms-safety training before anyone can be licensed, creating a mandatory customer base for instructors and training schools. That benefit rides on the same requirement gun owners experience as a cost.

industries.industry: State and local law enforcement agencies
industries.note: Agencies would receive federal grant money and would run registration, giving them new records for tracing crime guns. They would also carry the administrative burden of processing millions of registrations.
